title: How a process is told to stop

questions.question: You save a draft in onDestroy. It works every time in testing. Users still lose drafts. What is going wrong?
options: onDestroy runs on a background thread and the write is cut short
onDestroy is not called when the system reclaims the process
The draft is saved, then overwritten when the app restarts
onDestroy only runs for the last Activity in the task
questions.explanation: Testing ends the screen with Back or a rotation, and in both cases the process is alive to run the callback. The case you are trying to protect against removes the process, and there is nothing left to call anything.

questions.question: Which statement about SIGKILL is true?
options: A process can catch it and clean up quickly before it ends
It cannot be caught, so no code in the process runs after it arrives
It asks the runtime to write out a thread dump
It is only used when an app has already crashed
questions.explanation: The kernel does not allow a handler to be registered for it, so the process stops between two instructions. A signal a process could refuse would be useless for reclaiming memory, which is why this one is not negotiable.

questions.question: The user switches to another app, and twenty minutes later the system reclaims your process. Which of your callbacks ran?
options: onPause and onStop ran when the user left; onDestroy did not run
All three of onPause, onStop and onDestroy ran
Only onDestroy ran
None of them ran
questions.explanation: The callbacks you got happened twenty minutes earlier, when the user switched away, and that was the moment to have saved. By the time the process is reclaimed there is no code running to call anything else.

questions.question: Users report losing data, and your crash reporter shows nothing at all. Why?
options: The reporter cannot upload while the app is in the background
Nothing crashed. The process was ended, which is not an exception
The exception was swallowed inside a coroutine
The reporter only samples a fraction of sessions
questions.explanation: Process death produces no exception, so crash reporting has nothing to record and your crash-free rate stays perfect. To see it at all you have to read the system's record of why recent processes of your app ended.

questions.question: An ANR report contains what every thread in your app was doing. How was it produced?
options: The system reconstructs it from the last frames the app rendered
The runtime caught SIGQUIT, wrote the dump, and the process carried on
The app's crash handler wrote it just before the process died
The kernel dumps a process's memory whenever it kills it
questions.explanation: SIGQUIT can be caught, and the Android runtime catches it by writing the state of every thread and then continuing. That is why an ANR report is a snapshot of a living process and contains no exception.

questions.question: A user force stops your app from Settings. What happens to work you scheduled with WorkManager?
options: It continues, because scheduled work runs in the system process
It is cancelled permanently and has to be enqueued again from scratch
It does not run until the user launches the app again themselves
It runs, but only while the device is charging
questions.explanation: A force stop puts the app into a stopped state, and nothing scheduled by it fires while it is in that state. This is worth knowing because it looks exactly like a bug in your scheduling code and is not one.
